cue_condition.health.question: A 55-year-old male bodybuilder presents to the emergency department with weakness of his right arm. The patient states he has experienced these symptoms for a few weeks; however, today his hand felt so weak he dropped his cup of tea. The patient has a past medical history of diabetes. He drinks 2-7 alcoholic drinks per day and has smoked 2 packs of cigarettes per day since he was 25. The patient admits to using anabolic steroids. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 177/108 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Physical exam reveals decreased sensation in the right arm and 2/5 strength in the right arm and 5/5 strength in in the left arm. The patient states that he is experiencing a dull aching and burning pain in his right arm during the exam. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
He has lost 17 pounds since he last came to the emergency department 1 month ago.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has right arm weakness, decreased sensation, and dull aching/burning pain, suggesting a lower trunk brachial plexus lesion. The smoking history, unintentional weight loss, and right arm symptoms point to a Pancoast tumor (apical lung tumor) compressing the brachial plexus. This fits an apical lung tumor better than cerebral infarction, scalenus anticus syndrome, or subclavian steal syndrome.
Final answer: A

cue_condition.health.question:
A 33-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of fever and neck pain that radiates to the jaw and ears. She has also noticed swelling in the front part of her throat since the onset of the pain. She reports feeling anxious and sweating profusely over the past 2 days. She has no history of major illness and takes no medication. Her temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F), pulse is 95/min, and blood pressure is 140/70 mm Hg. Examination shows moist palms and a bilateral fine resting tremor of the outstretched hands. Examination of the neck shows a thyroid gland that is tender, firm, and enlarged. Serum studies show:
Hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL
ESR 65 mm/h
Serum
Creatinine 0.7 mg/dL
Thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.063 μU/mL
Triiodothyronine (T3) 218 ng/dL
Thyroxine (T4) 88 μg/dL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
123I scan shows an enlarged thyroid gland with multiple areas of decreased uptake

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has a tender, firm, enlarged thyroid with fever, neck pain radiating to the jaw and ears, and symptoms of hyperthyroidism. Laboratory findings show low TSH with elevated T3 and T4, and an elevated ESR. The 123I scan shows an enlarged thyroid with multiple areas of decreased uptake, which is characteristic of subacute thyroiditis (de Quervain thyroiditis).
Final answer: A

cue_condition.health.question: A 35-year-old woman presents to the ER with shortness of breath, cough, and severe lower limb enlargement. The dyspnea was of sudden onset, started a week ago, and increased with exercise but did not disappear with rest. Her cough was dry, persistent, and non-productive. She has a family history of maternal hypertension. Her vital signs include heart rate 106/min, respiratory rate 28/min, and blood pressure 140/90 mm Hg. On physical examination, thoracic expansion was diminished on the right side with rhonchi and crackles on the lower two-thirds of both sides, with left predominance. A systolic murmur was heard on the tricuspid foci, which increased in intensity with inspiration. There was jugular engorgement when the bed was placed at 50°. Palpation of the abdomen was painful on the right hypochondrium, with hepatomegaly 4 cm below the lower coastal edge. Hepatojugular reflux was present. Soft, painless, pitting edema was present in both lower limbs up until the middle third of both legs. What is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Lung computed tomography (CT) and transthoracic echocardiogram were performed and detected right heart failure and severe pulmonary fibrosis.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has signs of right heart failure (jugular engorgement, hepatomegaly, hepatojugular reflux, peripheral edema, tricuspid murmur) with pulmonary findings and a CT/echo showing right heart failure and severe pulmonary fibrosis. Right heart failure due to lung disease is cor pulmonale. Left-sided heart failure would typically show pulmonary congestion and left heart findings, not isolated right heart failure. Budd-Chiari syndrome causes hepatic venous outflow obstruction with ascites and hepatomegaly but not the pulmonary findings. Coronary artery disease is not directly supported by the presentation.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 72-year-old man is brought into clinic by his daughter for increasing confusion. The daughter states that over the past 2 weeks, she has noticed that the patient “seems to stare off into space.” She reports he has multiple episodes a day during which he will walk into a room and forget why. She is also worried about his balance. She endorses that he has had several falls, the worst being 3 weeks ago when he tripped on the sidewalk getting the mail. The patient denies loss of consciousness, pre-syncope, chest pain, palpitations, urinary incontinence, or bowel incontinence. He complains of headache but denies dizziness. He reports nausea and a few episodes of non-bloody emesis but denies abdominal pain, constipation, or diarrhea. The patient’s medical history is significant for atrial fibrillation, diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and osteoarthritis. He drinks a half glass of whisky after dinner every night and smokes a cigar on the weekends. On physical examination, he is oriented to name and place but not to date. He is unable to spell "world" backward. When asked to remember 3 words, he recalls only 2. There are no motor or sensory deficits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
He takes aspirin, warfarin, insulin, lisinopril, simvastatin, and ibuprofen.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has subacute cognitive decline, gait instability, and recent falls, along with headache and nausea. He is on warfarin and aspirin, which increase bleeding risk, and a fall 3 weeks ago could have caused a slow venous bleed. This presentation is most consistent with a chronic subdural hematoma. Alzheimer disease would be more gradual and less likely to cause acute gait changes or headache. Ischemic stroke would present with focal deficits, and vitamin B12 deficiency typically causes sensory changes and macrocytic anemia.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question:
A 44-year-old male immigrant presents to his primary care physician for a new patient visit. The patient reports chronic fatigue but states that he otherwise feels well. His past medical history is not known, and he is not currently taking any medications. The patient admits to drinking 7 alcoholic beverages per day and smoking 1 pack of cigarettes per day. His temperature is 99.4°F (37.4°C), blood pressure is 157/98 mmHg, pulse is 99/min, respirations are 18/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical exam demonstrates mild pallor but is otherwise not remarkable. Laboratory studies are ordered as seen below.

Hemoglobin: 9 g/dL
Hematocrit: 33%
Leukocyte count: 6,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 190,000/mm^3
Mean corpuscular volume (MCV): 60 femtoliters

Reticulocyte count: 2.8%

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Free iron: 272 mcg/dL
Total iron binding capacity (TIBC): 175 mcg/dL
Ferritin: 526 ng/mL

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has a microcytic anemia (MCV 60 fL) with a low-normal reticulocyte count. The iron studies show elevated ferritin and elevated free iron with low TIBC, which is not consistent with iron deficiency. Beta-thalassemia is a common cause of microcytic anemia with normal or elevated iron stores, especially in an immigrant patient. B12 deficiency and hemolytic anemia would typically present with macrocytic or normocytic anemia, respectively.
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question: A 37-year-old man comes to the emergency department with his wife because of a 3-day history of severe pain in his right arm. He also reports that he cannot move his right arm. The symptoms began after the patient woke up one morning, having slept on his side. He is otherwise healthy. He works as a waiter and says that he feels exhausted from working several night shifts per week. He adds that he “can barely keep his eyes open” when looking after their daughter the next day. Since the onset of the pain, he has been unable to work and is fully dependent on his wife, who took an extra shift to make enough money to pay their monthly bills. The patient appears relaxed but only allows himself to be examined after his wife convinces him. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows 1/5 muscle strength in the right arm. Reflexes are normal. He has no sensation to light touch over the entire right arm and forearm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
When a pin prick test is conducted, the patient rapidly withdraws the right arm.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient's symptoms of severe arm pain, weakness, and sensory loss after sleeping on his side suggest a peripheral nerve injury, but the rapid withdrawal to pin prick despite reported loss of light touch sensation is inconsistent with a complete sensory deficit. This inconsistency, along with the patient's reported inability to work and financial stressors, raises concern for intentional symptom production for external gain. The most likely diagnosis is malingering.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 30-year-old woman, gravida 4, para 3, at 39 weeks' gestation comes to the hospital 20 minutes after the onset of vaginal bleeding. She has not received prenatal care. Her third child was delivered by lower segment transverse cesarean section because of a footling breech presentation. Her other two children were delivered vaginally. Her temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F), pulse is 86/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 132/74 mm Hg. The abdomen is nontender, and no contractions are felt. The fetus is in a vertex presentation. The fetal heart rate is 96/min. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Per speculum examination reveals ruptured membranes and severe bleeding from the external os.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient presents with painless vaginal bleeding at term, a history of prior cesarean delivery, and a nonreassuring fetal heart rate. The additional finding of ruptured membranes with severe bleeding from the external os makes placenta previa less likely, as previa typically presents with intact membranes and bleeding from the placenta itself. Ruptured vasa previa is the most likely diagnosis because fetal vessels crossing the cervical os rupture when membranes break, causing fetal hemorrhage and fetal bradycardia.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of sudden loss of vision in her right eye that occurred 50 minutes ago. She does not have eye pain. She had several episodes of loss of vision in the past, but her vision improved following treatment with glucocorticoids. She has coronary artery disease, hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and multiple sclerosis. She underwent a left carotid endarterectomy 3 years ago. She had a myocardial infarction 5 years ago. Current medications include aspirin, metoprolol, lisinopril, atorvastatin, metformin, glipizide, and weekly intramuscular beta-interferon injections. Her temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F), pulse is 80/min, and blood pressure is 155/88 mm Hg. Examination shows 20/50 vision in the left eye and no perception of light in the right eye. The direct pupillary reflex is brisk in the left eye and absent in the right eye. The indirect pupillary reflex is brisk in the right eye but absent in the left eye. Intraocular pressure is 18 mm Hg in the right eye and 16 mm Hg in the left eye. A white, 1-mm ring is seen around the circumference of the cornea in both eyes. The optic disc appears normal. Fundoscopic examination of the left eye shows a few soft and hard exudates in the superior and nasal retinal quadrants. The optic disc and macula appear normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Fundoscopic examination of the right eye shows a pale, white retina with a bright red area within the macula.

reference_responses.intervention:
The sudden, painless, complete loss of vision in the right eye, absent direct pupillary reflex with a preserved indirect reflex, and the fundoscopic finding of a pale retina with a cherry-red spot at the macula are classic for central retinal artery occlusion. The patient's vascular risk factors (coronary artery disease, hypertension, diabetes, prior carotid surgery) support an embolic or thrombotic cause. The normal optic disc and intraocular pressure make acute angle-closure glaucoma unlikely, and the absence of visible blood in the vitreous or retinal detachment findings argues against vitreous hemorrhage or central serous retinopathy.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: An 11-year-old girl presents with a 1-day history of frothy brown urine. She has no significant medical history and takes no medications. She reports that several of her classmates have been sick, and . Her blood pressure is 146/94 mm Hg, heart rate is 74/min, and respiratory rate is 14/min. Laboratory analysis reveals elevated serum creatinine, hematuria with RBC casts, and elevated urine protein without frank proteinuria. Physical examination reveals a healthy-looking girl with no abdominal or costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
she notes that she had a very sore throat with a fever approx. 2 weeks ago

reference_responses.intervention:
The history of a sore throat with fever about 2 weeks ago, followed by frothy brown urine, hypertension, hematuria with RBC casts, and elevated serum creatinine is most consistent with poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. This condition typically occurs 1–3 weeks after a group A streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection. The presence of RBC casts indicates glomerular inflammation, and the latent period after pharyngitis supports this diagnosis over other causes. Alport syndrome is usually hereditary with sensorineural hearing loss and eye abnormalities, membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis often has nephrotic-range proteinuria and low complement, and Henoch-Schönlein purpura typically presents with palpable purpura, abdominal pain, and arthritis.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question:
A 67-year-old man refers to his physician for a follow-up examination. During his last visit 1 month ago, splenomegaly was detected. He has had night sweats for the past several months and has lost 5 kg (11 lb) unintentionally during this period. He has no history of severe illness and takes no medications. The vital signs are within normal limits. The examination shows no abnormalities other than splenomegaly. The laboratory studies show the following:
Hemoglobin 9 g/dL
Mean corpuscular volume 95 μm3
Leukocyte count 12,000/mm3
Platelet count 260,000/mm3
Ultrasound shows a spleen size of 15 cm and mild hepatomegaly. The marrow is very difficult to aspirate but reveals hyperplasia of all 3 lineages. The tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase (TRAP) test is negative. Clonal marrow plasma cells are not seen. JAK-2 is positive. The cytogenetic analysis is negative for translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
A peripheral blood smear shows teardrop-shaped and nucleated red blood cells (RBCs) and immature myeloid cells.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has anemia, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, a dry bone marrow tap with trilineage hyperplasia, a positive JAK2 mutation, and a peripheral blood smear showing teardrop cells, nucleated red blood cells, and immature myeloid cells. These findings are characteristic of primary myelofibrosis, especially in the prefibrotic or early fibrotic stage. The negative TRAP test and absence of clonal plasma cells argue against hairy cell leukemia and multiple myeloma, while the lack of erythrocytosis makes polycythemia vera unlikely. The cytogenetic absence of the Philadelphia chromosome excludes chronic myeloid leukemia.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 23-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a severe headache. The patient states he gets sudden, severe pain over his face whenever anything touches it, including shaving or putting lotion on his skin. He is currently pain free. His temperature is 98.1°F (36.7°C), blood pressure is 127/81 mmHg, pulse is 87/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. Neurological exam is within normal limits, except severe pain is elicited with light palpation of the patient’s face. The patient is requesting morphine for his pain. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
He describes the pain as electric and states it is only exacerbated by touch.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient's pain is triggered by light touch, such as shaving or applying lotion, and is described as electric, which is characteristic of trigeminal neuralgia. The neurological exam is otherwise normal, and the pain is currently absent between episodes. Cluster, migraine, and tension headaches do not typically present with touch-evoked, electric facial pain. Therefore, trigeminal neuralgia is the most likely diagnosis.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 2-year-old female with abdominal pain undergoes laparoscopic surgery. An outpouching of tissue is excised from the ileum and sent to the laboratory for evaluation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
The pathologist notes inflammation and the presence of mucosa, submucosa, and muscle in the walls of the specimen.

reference_responses.intervention:
The specimen is an outpouching of the ileum containing all three layers (mucosa, submucosa, and muscle), which is characteristic of a true diverticulum. Meckel's diverticulum is a true diverticulum of the ileum and is the most common congenital anomaly of the gastrointestinal tract. Crohn's disease and Henoch-Schonlein purpura do not present as a discrete ileal outpouching with all bowel wall layers, and appendicitis involves the appendix rather than the ileum.
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question:
A 14-year-old girl is referred to a gynecologist for amenorrhea. Her mother is also concerned that she hasn't grown any hair "in her private parts." The patient states that she is getting used to high school and wants to join the volleyball team but complains that her weakness and headaches limit her physical activity. She does not share her mother's concerns about her menses. She reveals that her parents are maternal cousins. Her cardiac exam is unremarkable, and her abdominal exam reveals no bruits. After obtaining permission for a pelvic exam, the exam reveals a normal appearing vagina without any hair. No cervical os can be palpated. Initial labs reveal the following:

Serum:
Na+: 143 mEq/L
Cl-: 110 mEq/L
K+: 2.9 mEq/L
HCO3-: 26 mEq/L
BUN: 40 mg/dL
Glucose: 104 mg/dL
Creatinine: 1.3 mg/dL

What is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Her temperature is 98°F (37°C), blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg, pulse is 70/min, and respirations are 24/min.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has primary amenorrhea, absent pubic hair, hypertension, hypokalemia, and metabolic alkalosis, which are characteristic of 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency. This enzyme defect impairs cortisol and sex steroid synthesis, causing mineralocorticoid excess and absent secondary sexual characteristics. The elevated blood pressure and low potassium support mineralocorticoid excess rather than a virilizing enzyme defect. The other listed enzyme deficiencies typically present with ambiguous genitalia or virilization, not absent pubic hair with hypertension.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question:
A 58-year-old woman presents to the clinic with an abnormal sensation on the left side of her body that has been present for the past several months. At first, the area seemed numb and she recalls touching a hot stove and accidentally burning herself but not feeling the heat. Now she is suffering from a constant, uncomfortable burning pain on her left side for the past week. The pain gets worse when someone even lightly touches that side. She has recently immigrated and her past medical records are unavailable. She confirms a history of hypertension, type II diabetes mellitus, and bilateral knee pain. She also had cardiac surgery 20 years ago. She denies fever, mood changes, weight changes, and trauma to the head, neck, or limbs. Her blood pressure is 162/90 mm Hg, the heart rate is 82/min, and the respiratory rate is 15/min. Multiple old burn marks are visible on the left hand and forearm. Muscle strength is mildly reduced in the left upper and lower limbs. Hyperesthesia is noted in the left upper and lower limbs. Laboratory results are significant for:
Hemoglobin 13.9 g/dL
MCV 92 fL
White blood cells 7,500/mm3
Platelets 278,000/mm3
Creatinine 1.3 U/L
BUN 38 mg/dL
TSH 2.5 uU/L
Hemoglobin A1c 7.9%
Vitamin B12 526 ng/L
What is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Last month she had a stroke but she cannot recall any details from the event.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has a history of stroke and now presents with left-sided sensory loss and subsequent constant burning pain, with hyperesthesia and allodynia (pain from light touch). This pattern is consistent with central post-stroke pain, also known as Dejerine-Roussy syndrome, which typically follows a thalamic or other central sensory pathway lesion. Complex regional pain syndrome usually follows limb trauma or surgery and is not explained by a stroke, while conversion disorder and medial medullary syndrome do not fit the unilateral sensory loss with burning pain after stroke.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 23-year-old woman presents to the emergency room for a self-inflicted laceration of her distal volar forearm. In the emergency department the bleeding is stopped and the patient is currently medically stable. When interviewing the patient, she is teary and apologizes for her behavior. She is grateful to you for her care and regrets her actions. Of note, the patient has presented to the emergency department before for a similar reason when she was struggling with online dating. The patient states that she struggles with her romantic relationship though she deeply desires them. On physical exam you note a frightened young woman who is wearing a revealing dress that prominently displays her breasts. You tell the patient that she will have to stay in the psychiatric emergency department for the night which makes her furious. Which of the following personality disorders is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
The patient states that she knew her husband was having sexual thoughts about the woman from the grocery store, prompting her decision to cut her own wrist.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient shows recurrent self-harm, emotional instability, intense anger when feeling abandoned or controlled, and unstable relationships, which are core features of borderline personality disorder. The additional statement about believing her husband had sexual thoughts about another woman and cutting her wrist reflects a pattern of impulsive self-harm in response to perceived interpersonal threat, consistent with borderline pathology. Histrionic, avoidant, and dependent personality disorders do not account for the self-injurious behavior and emotional dysregulation seen here.
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question: A 28-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after being found in a confused state on an interstate rest area in Florida. She is unable to recall her name, address, or any other information regarding her person. She denies being the woman on a Connecticut driver's license found in her wallet. A telephone call with the police department of her hometown reveals that she had been reported missing three days ago by her husband. When the husband arrives, he reports that his wife has had a great deal of stress at work lately and before she went missing, was anxious to tell her boss that she will not meet the deadline for her current project. She has had two major depressive episodes within the past 4 years that were treated with citalopram. She drinks one to two beers daily and sometimes more on weekends. She does not use illicit drugs. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical and neurological examinations show no abnormalities. On mental status exam, she is oriented only to time and place but not to person. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Short-term memory is intact; she does not recognize her husband or recall important events of her life.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has a loss of personal identity and autobiographical memory (oriented to time and place but not person) after a stressful event, with no evidence of delirium, substance intoxication, or neurological deficit. Short-term memory is intact, which argues against Korsakoff syndrome, and the lack of depersonalization symptoms makes depersonalization disorder less likely. The wandering away from home with inability to recall her past is consistent with dissociative amnesia with dissociative fugue.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of left testicular swelling. He has no pain. He underwent a left inguinal hernia repair as a child. He takes no medications. He appears healthy. His vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows an enlarged, nontender left testicle. When the patient is asked to cough, there is no bulge present in the scrotum. When a light is held behind the scrotum, it does not shine through. There is no inguinal lymphadenopathy.

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Laboratory studies show:
Hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL
Leukocyte count 8,800/mm3
Platelet count 345,000/mm3
Serum
Glucose 88 mg/dL
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL
Alkaline phosphatase 35 U/L
AST 15 U/L
ALT 14 U/L
Lactate dehydrogenase 60 U/L
β-Human chorionic gonadotropin 80 mIU/mL (N < 5)
α-Fetoprotein 6 ng/mL (N < 10)
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has a painless, solid testicular mass with no transillumination and no hernia bulge, consistent with a testicular tumor. The elevated β-hCG with normal α-fetoprotein and normal LDH is most characteristic of a seminoma, which can produce β-hCG but not α-fetoprotein. Choriocarcinoma would typically cause much higher β-hCG, and yolk sac tumor would elevate α-fetoprotein. A spermatocele would transilluminate and is a cystic lesion.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 76-year-old woman is brought to the physician because of lesions on her left arm. She first noticed them 3 months ago and they have grown larger since that time. She has not had any pain or pruritus in the area. Physical examination shows extensive edema of the left arm. There are four coalescing, firm, purple-blue nodules on the left lateral axillary region and swelling of the surrounding skin. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
She has a history of invasive ductal carcinoma of the left breast, which was treated with mastectomy and radiation therapy 27 years ago. Since that time, she has had lymphedema of the left arm.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has chronic lymphedema of the left arm following mastectomy and radiation therapy for breast cancer 27 years ago. She now presents with purple-blue nodules and surrounding skin swelling in the lymphedematous area. This clinical picture is most consistent with angiosarcoma arising in chronic lymphedema (Stewart-Treves syndrome).
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after a motor vehicle accident. He was the unrestrained front seat driver in a head on collision. The patient is unresponsive and his medical history is unknown. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 67/38 mmHg, pulse is 190/min, respirations are 33/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. The patient is started on IV fluids, blood products, and norepinephrine. A FAST exam is performed and a pelvic binder is placed. One hour later, his temperature is 98.3°F (36.8°C), blood pressure is 119/66 mmHg, pulse is 110/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 97% on room air. The patient is currently responsive. Management of the patient's pelvic fracture is scheduled by the orthopedic service. While the patient is waiting in the emergency department he suddenly complains of feeling hot, aches, and a headache. The patient's temperature is currently 101°F (38.3°C). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
He has not been given any pain medications and his past medical history is still unknown.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient received blood products during resuscitation and later developed fever, chills, and headache without evidence of hemolysis or hypotension. This presentation is most consistent with a febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction, which is caused by cytokines or recipient antibodies reacting to donor leukocytes. An acute hemolytic transfusion reaction would typically cause fever, hypotension, and hemoglobinuria, but the patient is now hemodynamically stable. Leukoagglutination is a mechanism underlying febrile non-hemolytic reactions rather than a separate diagnosis, and minor blood group incompatibility would more likely cause a delayed hemolytic reaction.
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to the physician because of repetitive tongue twisting and abnormal movements of the hands and legs that started several days ago. She has a 2-year history of schizophrenia that has been controlled with fluphenazine. Two weeks ago, she was switched to risperidone. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Examination shows protrusion of the tongue and smacking of the lips. She makes twisting movements of the arms and frequently taps her right foot.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has repetitive, involuntary movements of the tongue, lips, arms, and legs after long-term antipsychotic use and a recent medication switch. These movements are characteristic of tardive dyskinesia, a delayed-onset movement disorder caused by chronic dopamine receptor blockade. The recent switch from fluphenazine to risperidone does not eliminate the risk and may unmask or worsen the dyskinesia. Cerebellar stroke, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, and akathisia do not match the described choreoathetoid movements.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by the police after he was found running around a local park naked and screaming late at night. During intake, the patient talks non-stop about the government spying on him and his family, but provides little useful information besides his name and date of birth. Occasionally he refers to himself in the third person. He refuses to eat anything and will only drink clear fluids because he is afraid of being poisoned. Today, his heart rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 19/min, blood pressure is 135/85 mm Hg, and temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). On physical exam, he appears gaunt and anxious. His heart has a regular rate and rhythm and his lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. CMP, CBC, and TSH are normal. A urine toxicology test is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
A medical records search reveals that the patient has been treated for psychotic behavior and occasional bouts of severe depression for several years.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has had psychotic symptoms and recurrent severe depression for several years, which is most consistent with schizoaffective disorder. Schizophrenia would not explain the prominent mood episodes, and brief psychotic disorder requires symptoms lasting less than one month. Bipolar 1 disorder can include psychosis, but the psychosis here is present outside of mood episodes and has been chronic.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the physician by her parents for the evaluation of pubic hair development. She has a history of a fracture in each leg and one fracture in her right arm. Her performance at school is good. There is no family history of serious illness. She takes no medications. Vital signs are within normal limits. Genital examination shows coarse, dark hair along the labia. The breast glands are enlarged and the breast bud extends beyond the areolar diameter. The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:

Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination of the right lower extremity shows intact skin. The posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable. When pressure is applied to the sole of the foot between the metatarsal heads the patient feels pain and there is an audible click. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Tapping on the affected area causes pain that shoots into the third and fourth digits.

The additional finding of tapping the affected area causing shooting pain into the third and fourth digits is a positive Tinel-like sign, further supporting nerve entrapment. A stress fracture would typically cause localized bony pain with weight-bearing, not radiating neuropathic pain or a click. Osteochondrosis and osteomyelitis do not present with this pattern of interdigital nerve symptoms.

A 46-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination. Two weeks ago, he underwent laparoscopic herniorrhaphy for an indirect inguinal hernia. He has a history of intermittent scleral icterus that resolved without treatment. Serum studies show:

cue_condition.health.question: A 63-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of progressive blurring and darkening of her vision in the right eye. She has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years. Her only medication is sumatriptan. Her vitals are within normal limits. cue_condition.health.question: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of blisters on her forearms and pain during sexual intercourse. cue_condition.health.question: A 35-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-month history of double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and weakness when trying to brush her hair. She reports that these symptoms are worse after she exercises and disappear after she rests for a few hours. There is diminished motor strength in the upper extremities. Physical examination shows drooping of her right upper eyelid that worsens when the patient is asked to gaze at the ceiling for 2 minutes.

cue_condition.health.question: A 57-year-old man presents with 2 days of severe, generalized, abdominal pain that is worse after meals. cue_condition.health.question: A 69-year-old man presents to his primary care physician for pain when he walks. A mutation on his chromosome 9 confirms the physician’s suspicion of a certain clonal myeloproliferative disease.

cue_condition.health.question: A 34-year-old Ethiopian woman who recently moved to the United States presents for evaluation to a surgical outpatient clinic with painful ulceration in her right breast for the last 2 months. cue_condition.health.question: A 15-year-old girl is brought into her pediatrician's office by her mother because the mother thinks her daughter has attention issues. The mother explains that her daughter started high school four months ago and had lackluster grades in a recent progress report despite having earned consistent top marks in middle school. The mother complains that her daughter never talks to her at home anymore. The patient scoffs that her mother is so overbeaing, ruining her good days with criticism. She begins to chew gum and states that she hates hanging out with the girls on the cheerleading squad. She denies experiencing physical abuse from anyone or having a sexual partner. She has seen kids smoke marijuana underneath the football field bleachers, but does not go near them and denies smoking cigarettes. She denies any intention to harm herself or others, thinks her grades went down because her teachers are not as good as her middle school teachers, and states she thinks she learns best by watching explanations through online videos. Oppositional defiant disorder requires a persistent pattern of angry/irritable mood, argumentative/defiant behavior, or vindictiveness lasting at least six months, and conduct disorder requires a repetitive pattern of violating others' rights or major rules. Antisocial personality disorder cannot be diagnosed before age 18. The additional evidence of yelling at her mother in the exam room is a single episode and does not establish a persistent pattern. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is normal adolescent behavior.

cue_condition.health.question: A 78-year-old man presents to the hospital because of shortness of breath and chest pain that started a few hours ago. 3 weeks ago he had surgery for a total hip replacement with a prosthesis. cue_condition.health.question: A 24-day-old infant girl is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-hour history of fever, vomiting, and diarrhea. She has fed less and has had decreased urine output for 1 day. She was born at 33 weeks' gestation and weighed 1400-g (3-lb 1-oz). Her diet consists of breast milk and cow milk protein-based formula. Examination shows abdominal rigidity, distention, and absent bowel sounds. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The additional finding of pneumatosis intestinalis (gas within the intestinal wall) and pneumoperitoneum (gas in the peritoneal cavity) on abdominal x-ray strongly supports this diagnosis. Meckel diverticulum, cow milk protein allergy, and Hirschsprung disease do not typically present with this acute systemic illness and radiographic pattern in a preterm neonate.

cue_condition.health.question: A 39-year-old woman comes to the physician for difficulty sleeping and poor concentration at work. PTSD requires symptoms for more than one month, and adjustment disorder does not involve the specific re-experiencing and avoidance seen here.

cue_condition.health.question: A 6-week-old girl is brought to a pediatrician due to feeding difficulty for the last 4 days. choices.C: Supracristal ventricular septal defect with aortic regurgitation
choices.D: Ruptured congenital sinus of Valsalva aneurysm

The murmur obscures S2 and peaks at end-systole, consistent with a continuous machinery-like murmur. Other options are less likely because they typically produce different murmurs or presentations.

cue_condition.health.question: A 70-year-old man is accompanied by his wife to the primary care clinic for hand tremors. He states that he first noticed the tremor of his left hand 1 year ago. cue_condition.health.question: A 65-year-old woman presents to the clinic for a routine checkup. She has unintentionally lost 4.5 kg (9.9 lb) in the past month but denies any other complaints. Her pulse rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 18/min, temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), and blood pressure is 150/70 mm Hg. An irregularly irregular rhythm is heard on auscultation of the heart. Neck examination shows a markedly enlarged thyroid with no lymphadenopathy or bruit. Laboratory tests show low serum thyroid-stimulating hormone level, high T4 level, absent thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin, and absent anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody. Nuclear scintigraphy shows patchy uptake with multiple hot and cold areas.

The patient has clinical and laboratory evidence of hyperthyroidism (weight loss, tachycardia, low TSH, high T4) with an enlarged thyroid and no thyroid autoantibodies. The nuclear scintigraphy finding of patchy uptake with multiple hot and cold areas is characteristic of toxic multinodular goiter, where autonomous nodules produce excess thyroid hormone while other areas are suppressed. Graves' disease typically shows diffuse increased uptake and positive thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulin; Hashimoto's thyroiditis is usually associated with hypothyroidism and positive anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody; subacute granulomatous thyroiditis typically presents with a painful tender thyroid and low radioactive iodine uptake. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is toxic multinodular goiter.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 48-year-old woman presents to an urgent care clinic with the complaints of bloody diarrhea, mid-abdominal discomfort, and cramping for 3 days. cue_condition.health.question: A 68-year-old man comes to the physician for evaluation of a lump in his left axilla that he first noticed 1 year ago. Hodgkin lymphoma typically presents with contiguous lymphadenopathy and Reed-Sternberg cells, while Burkitt lymphoma is aggressive and associated with t(8;14). Marginal zone lymphoma is not associated with t(14;18).

cue_condition.health.question: A 17-year-old girl comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of pain in her right knee. Last week she had right wrist pain. She has no history of recent trauma. cue_condition.health.question: A 30-year-old primigravida schedules an appointment with her obstetrician for a regular check-up. She says that everything is fine, although she reports that her baby has stopped moving as much as previously. She is 22 weeks gestation. She denies any pain or vaginal bleeding. The obstetrician performs an ultrasound and also orders routine blood and urine tests. The patient is asked to wait for 1 hour, after which the scan is to be repeated. cue_condition.health.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with fever, diarrhea and bilateral red eye for 7 days. C. difficile colitis is unlikely without recent antibiotic use, and Vibrio parahaemolyticus is associated with seafood ingestion, not daycare outbreaks.

cue_condition.health.question: A 67-year-old man presents to the emergency department for a headache. The patient states his symptoms started thirty minutes ago. He states he experienced a sudden and severe headache while painting his house, causing him to fall of the ladder and hit his head. He has also experienced two episodes of vomiting and difficulty walking since the fall. The patient has a past medical history of hypertension, obesity, and atrial fibrillation. His current medications include lisinopril, rivaroxaban, atorvastatin, and metformin. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 150/105 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 15/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. On physical exam, the patient localizes his headache to the back of his head. Cardiac exam reveals a normal rate and rhythm. Pulmonary exam reveals minor bibasilar crackles. Neurological exam is notable for minor weakness of the muscles of facial expression. Examination of cranial nerve three reveals a notable nystagmus. A non-contrast CT scan of the head is currently pending. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

reference_responses.intervention:

Cerebellar hemorrhage commonly presents with occipital headache, gait ataxia, and limb incoordination, and can cause nausea and vomiting. The fall from the ladder may be secondary to the hemorrhage rather than the cause of symptoms. While subarachnoid hemorrhage is a consideration with sudden headache, the prominent cerebellar signs make cerebellar hemorrhage more likely.
Final answer: A

cue_condition.health.question: A 32-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of worsening shortness of breath and a productive cough for 3 days. cue_condition.health.question: A 25-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 4-day history of bloody stools. His father died of colon cancer at the age of 39 years. His vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows small, painless bony swellings on the mandible, forehead, and right shin. reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has multiple colonic polyps, osteomas (painless bony swellings on mandible, forehead, shin), epidermoid cysts (subcutaneous nodules with central black pores), and congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (oval darkly pigmented retinal lesions). Cronkhite-Canada syndrome typically presents with diarrhea, alopecia, nail changes, and hyperpigmentation, not osteomas or retinal lesions. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome features hamartomatous polyps and mucocutaneous pigmentation, while Cowden syndrome is associated with trichilemmomas and increased risk of breast, thyroid, and endometrial cancers.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 4430-g (9-lb 10-oz) male newborn is delivered at term to a 27-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1. The second stage of labor was prolonged and required vacuum-assisted vaginal delivery. Apgar scores are 9 and 10 at 1 and 5 minutes, respectively. Vital signs are within normal limits. A subgaleal hemorrhage would cross suture lines and may be more diffuse, while a lipoma or epidermoid cyst would not typically present acutely after vacuum-assisted delivery. The vacuum-assisted delivery and prolonged second stage are risk factors for cephalohematoma.

cue_condition.health.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with erosions in her mouth that are persistent and painful. She says that symptoms appeared gradually 1 week ago and have progressively worsened. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

She claims that her husband frequently makes a scene and apologizes for her husband's behavior. On mental status examination, the patient is oriented to person, place, and time. He appears agitated and speaks in short, pressured sentences. There is no disorder of thought process or content. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

cue_condition.health.question: A 19-year-old man and recent immigrant from Brazil present to the clinic. He has no known past medical, past surgical, or family history. The patient admits to having several regular sexual partners. Today, he complains of a skin rash on his back. He is unclear when it started but became aware when one of his partners pointed it out. cue_condition.health.question: A 22-year-old student presents to the college health clinic with a 1-week history of fever, sore throat, nausea, and fatigue. He could hardly get out of bed this morning. There are no pets at home. He admits to having recent unprotected sex. The vital signs include: temperature 38.3°C (101.0°F), pulse 72/min, blood pressure 118/63 mm Hg, and respiratory rate 15/min. What is the most likely diagnosis?

cue_condition.health.question: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician for a follow-up examination one week after a chest x-ray showed a solitary pulmonary nodule. cue_condition.health.question: A 58-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 3-month history of diffuse muscle pain, malaise, pain in both knees, recurrent episodes of abdominal and chest pain. cue_condition.health.question: A 43-year-old Caucasian female with a long history of uncontrolled migraines presents to general medical clinic with painless hematuria. Painless hematuria with an elevated creatinine and biopsy findings of papillary necrosis and tubulointerstitial infiltrate are classic features of analgesic nephropathy. Kidney stones typically cause flank pain and colicky pain, bladder cancer is associated with risk factors like smoking and usually presents with irritative voiding symptoms, and sickle cell disease would show other systemic findings and is less likely in a Caucasian female without a suggestive history.

cue_condition.health.question: A 32-year-old woman presents to the emergency department due to severe, intractable headaches, and bilateral ocular pain. She initially had right-sided headaches that were sharp, interfered with sleep, and were unresponsive to pain medications. The headache was around her right eye and cheek, and she noticed diplopia with right lateral gaze. Her symptoms were accompanied by fatigue, fever, and edema around the right eye. Approximately 2 days after these symptoms, she developed swelling around the left eye. Medical history is significant for a recent rhinosinusitis infection. Her temperature is 101°F (38.3°C), blood pressure is 133/72 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, and respirations are 18/min. On physical exam, there is ptosis, proptosis, chemosis, and periorbital swelling of both eyes. Fundoscopic exam demonstrates bilateral papilledema. Bilateral involvement, papilledema, and cranial nerve deficits (including trigeminal hyperesthesia in V1/V2) are classic for cavernous sinus thrombosis, whereas orbital cellulitis is usually unilateral and less likely to cause bilateral papilledema or extensive cranial nerve involvement. Acute angle-closure glaucoma would present with a fixed mid-dilated pupil, severe eye pain, and elevated intraocular pressure, not bilateral proptosis and ophthalmoplegia. Bacterial endophthalmitis typically follows intraocular surgery or trauma and presents with intraocular inflammation, not bilateral orbital signs.

cue_condition.health.question: A 34-year-old female presents to a counselor at the urging of her parents because they are concerned that she might be depressed. She describes feeling uneasy when she is alone. She has hypothyroidism treated with levothyroxine. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. Vital signs are normal. Mental status exam shows a neutral affect. Neurologic examination shows no focal findings. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

After recently breaking up with her long-term boyfriend, she moved back in with her parents because she could not handle making decisions alone.

Her unemployment, reliance on her mother for appointments and car maintenance, and moving back with parents after the breakup reflect this pattern. These features are most consistent with dependent personality disorder rather than separation anxiety disorder, which centers on anxiety about separation from attachment figures, or histrionic or borderline personality disorder.

cue_condition.health.question: A 20-year-old man presents with a painless neck mass that has gradually increased in size. The mass increased in size and became more tender following an upper respiratory infection. An ultrasound of the neck identifies a single, round cystic mass with uniform, low echogenicity, and no internal septations. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the neck shows a homogeneous mass with low attenuation centrally and with smooth rim enhancement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The location anteromedial to the sternocleidomastoid muscle and the long duration of 3 years further support this diagnosis. First branchial cleft cysts are typically near the ear or angle of the mandible, ectopic thyroid tissue is usually solid and midline, and a sternomastoid tumor presents in infancy.

cue_condition.health.question: A 37-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 15 minutes after falling down a flight of stairs. She is otherwise healthy. She takes no medications. On arrival, she has shortness of breath, right-sided chest pain, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and right shoulder pain.

reference_responses.intervention:

Right shoulder pain (Kehr sign) indicates diaphragmatic irritation, commonly from blood from a liver injury. A liver hematoma is more likely than splenic laceration because the pain is right-sided and the right chest wall is also bruised.

cue_condition.health.question: Two days following the home birth of her son, a mother brings the infant to the pediatric emergency room because of bilious vomiting. He is unable to pass meconium and his abdomen is distended. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

This condition causes functional obstruction because the aganglionic segment cannot relax. The other listed conditions do not present with neonatal bilious vomiting and absent ganglion cells on biopsy.

cue_condition.health.question: A 4-year-old girl presents to the office with her parents who are concerned about their daughter and slow, progressive changes in her behavior. The vital signs include: heart rate 90/min, respiratory rate 22/min, blood pressure 110/65 mm Hg, and temperature 36.9°C (98.4°F). At one point she had a vocabulary of several words and now she verbalizes in grunts. She also flaps her hands in a repeated motion and has difficulty walking.

Autistic spectrum disorder does not classically involve loss of previously acquired skills and motor regression, and phenylketonuria or Tourette syndrome would not explain this pattern.

cue_condition.health.question: Six hours after delivery, a 3100-g (6-lb 13-oz) male newborn has an episode of bilious projectile vomiting. He was born at term to a 21-year-old woman. Duodenal atresia typically shows a double bubble sign, meconium ileus often has a soap-bubble appearance with distal obstruction, and Hirschsprung disease usually presents with delayed meconium passage and distal colonic dilation. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is jejunal atresia.

cue_condition.health.question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the emergency room for evaluation of malaise, dyspnea, and yellow skin and sclera. On examination, he is tachycardic, tachypneic, and the O2 saturation is less than 90%. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Placenta previa usually presents with painless bleeding, and uterine rupture is less likely with an unscarred uterus and normal ultrasound.

cue_condition.health.question: A previously healthy 64-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a dry cough and progressively worsening shortness of breath for the past 2 months. Lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis are typically painless, and fibrous thyroiditis (Riedel) is hard and fixed, not tender. The dysphagia and anxiety about esophageal cancer are secondary to the thyroid swelling, not a primary esophageal malignancy.

cue_condition.health.question: A newborn born at 33 weeks of gestation has a respiratory rate of 70/min and a heart rate of 148/min 2 hours after birth. He is grunting and has intercostal and subcostal retractions. He has peripheral cyanosis as well. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Transient tachypnea of the newborn typically shows fluid in the fissures and perihilar streaking, not a ground-glass appearance. cue_condition.health.question: A 37-year-old machinist presents to his primary care physician with eye problems. The patient states that he has had a mass in his eye that has persisted for the past month. The patient has a past medical history of blepharitis treated with eye cleansing and squamous cell carcinoma of the skin treated with Mohs surgery. His temperature is 99.5°F (37.5°C), blood pressure is 157/102 mmHg, pulse is 90/min, respirations are 17/min, and oxygen saturation is 98% on room air. cue_condition.health.question: A 20-year-old man comes to the physician because he believes he has low testosterone. He states that he is embarrassed at his lack of musculature, despite lifting weights twice daily. Every day, he drinks a gallon of milk and several protein shakes in addition to 3 large meals. He is convinced that his female classmates at the community college he attends are secretly laughing at his scrawny appearance. Over the course of the semester, he has attended fewer and fewer classes out of embarrassment and shame. He is also concerned that his hair is thinning and applies topical minoxidil to his scalp 3 times daily. Today, he is wearing a long-sleeved shirt and a hat. His BMI is 26 kg/m2. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. On mental status examination, he has an anxious mood and a full range of affect. Serum studies show a normal testosterone concentration. Consider this additional source evidence:
He spends 2 hours daily anxiously examining himself in the mirror.

Avoidant personality disorder is characterized by a broader pattern of social inhibition and feelings of inadequacy, not a specific focus on appearance. Binge eating disorder involves recurrent episodes of eating large amounts with loss of control, which is not described. Generalized anxiety disorder involves excessive worry about multiple domains, not a focused preoccupation with appearance.

cue_condition.health.question: A 24-year-old woman comes to her physician because of fatigue. She has been coming to the office multiple times a month for various minor problems over the past six months. During the appointments, When the physician tells her politely that her behavior is inappropriate, she begins to cry, complaining that no one understands her and that if people only listened to her, she would not be so exhausted. She then quickly gathers herself and states that she will just have to keep looking for a physician who can help her, although she has doubts she will ever find the right physician. She does not have a history of self harm or suicidal ideation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

she insists on a first name basis and flirts with her physician. She always dresses very fashionably. When his assistant enters the room, she tends to start fidgeting and interrupt their conversation.

There is no evidence of the identity disturbance, chronic emptiness, or self-harm that would suggest borderline personality disorder, nor the submissive clinging of dependent personality disorder or the odd beliefs and social detachment of schizotypal personality disorder.

cue_condition.health.question: A 19-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 2-day history of difficulty sleeping. Her extravagant dress and flirtatious behavior with the receptionist further support this diagnosis. Dependent personality disorder would center on submissive clinging and fear of separation, while narcissistic personality disorder would involve grandiosity and lack of empathy. cue_condition.health.question: A 40-year-old nulliparous woman with no significant medical history presents to your office with shortness of breath and increased abdominal girth over the past month. cue_condition.health.question: A 65-year-old woman comes to the clinic for an annual well-check. cue_condition.health.question: A 9-year-old boy is brought to the office due to exertional dyspnea and fatigability. He tires easily when walking or playing. This explains the exertional dyspnea, fatigability, and differential cyanosis.

His mother does not provide any history of similar symptoms in the past. Past medical history is non-significant. His birth history is uneventful and all his vaccinations are up to date. The vital signs include: blood pressure 100/62 mm Hg, pulse 110/min, temperature 36.7°C (98.0°F), and respiratory rate 16/min. On examination, there is pitting edema of the upper and lower extremities bilaterally.
 Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
Urinalysis results are as follows:
pH 6.2
Color light yellow
RBC none
WBC 3–4/HPF
Protein 4+
Cast Fat globules
Glucose absent
Crystal none
Ketone absent
Nitrite absent
24-hour urine protein excretion 4.1 g
A renal biopsy is sent which shows normal glomeruli on light microscopy.

reference_responses.intervention:
The child has nephrotic-range proteinuria (4.1 g/day), edema, frothy urine, and a renal biopsy with normal glomeruli on light microscopy. In a young child, this presentation is most consistent with minimal change disease, also known as lipoid nephrosis. The other options typically show abnormal glomerular findings on light microscopy or are less common in this age group.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 63-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic complaining of severe vulvar itching. The pruritus started 1 year ago and became worse over the last several months. She has tried over-the-counter topical steroids without relief. She is not currently sexually active. Her medical history is notable for long-standing lichen sclerosus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Consider this additional source evidence:
The physical examination reveals an ulcerated small nodule on the right labium majus, as well as dry, thin, white lesions encircling the genital and perianal areas.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has long-standing lichen sclerosus, which is a known risk factor for vulvar squamous cell carcinoma. The new ulcerated nodule on the labium majus is concerning for malignant transformation. Bartholin gland cyst or carcinoma would present as a mass in the Bartholin gland area, not as an ulcerated nodule with surrounding lichen sclerosus changes. Vulvar Paget's disease typically presents as an eczematous, red, weeping plaque rather than an ulcerated nodule.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question: A 25-year-old woman comes to the physician for the evaluation of blindness in her right eye that suddenly started 1 hour ago. She has no feeling of pain, pressure, or sensation of a foreign body in the right eye. She has a history of major depressive disorder treated with fluoxetine. The patient attends college and states that she has had a lot of stress lately due to relationship problems with her partner. She does not smoke or drink alcohol. She does not use illicit drugs. She appears anxious. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Ophthalmologic examination shows a normal-appearing eye with no redness. Slit lamp examination and fundoscopy show no abnormalities. An MRI of the brain shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

intervention.text:
Consider this additional source evidence:
A visual field test shows nonspecific visual field defects.

reference_responses.intervention:
The sudden, painless monocular blindness with a normal ophthalmologic examination, slit lamp, fundoscopy, and brain MRI, along with nonspecific visual field defects, is most consistent with a functional neurological symptom disorder. Retinal detachment would typically show fundoscopic abnormalities, and malingering requires evidence of intentional feigning for external gain, which is not described. Somatic symptom disorder involves persistent somatic symptoms with excessive thoughts, feelings, or behaviors, but the acute, isolated visual loss is better explained by conversion disorder.
Final answer: D

cue_condition.health.question: A 17-year-old boy presents to his primary care physician for eye pain. The patient states that it has been going on for the past 3 days and has been steadily worsening. He recently suffered a superior orbital fracture secondary to playing football without a helmet that required no treatment other than to refrain from contact sports. That patient's past medical history is non-contributory, and his vitals are within normal limits. Physical exam demonstrates pain and swelling inferior to the patient's eye near the lacrimal duct. Cranial nerves II-XII are grossly intact. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

This localized finding points to an infection of the lacrimal sac rather than a more diffuse eyelid or orbital process. Dacryocystitis commonly presents with tenderness, erythema, and purulent discharge at the medial canthus, often after nasolacrimal duct obstruction. The recent orbital fracture is not directly causative here, and the intact cranial nerve exam makes orbital cellulitis less likely.

cue_condition.health.question: A 27-year-old woman presents to her family physician with pain on the front of her right knee. The pain started 2 months ago after she began training for a marathon, and it was gradual in onset and has slowly worsened. The pain increases with prolonged sitting and climbing stairs. She denies significant knee trauma. Her only medication is diclofenac sodium as needed for pain. Medical history is unremarkable. The vital signs include: temperature 36.9°C (98.4°F), blood pressure 100/70 mm Hg, and heart rate 78/min. Her body mass index is 26 kg/m2. The remainder of the examination is otherwise unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The additional finding of pain with direct pressure on the patella and increased patellar laxity supports patellofemoral tracking issues rather than iliotibial band syndrome, prepatellar bursitis, or Osgood-Schlatter's disease. Iliotibial band syndrome typically causes lateral knee pain, prepatellar bursitis causes focal swelling and pain over the patella without laxity, and Osgood-Schlatter's disease occurs in adolescents with tibial tubercle pain.
Final answer: C

cue_condition.health.question:
A 34-year-old man presents to a clinic with complaints of abdominal discomfort and blood in the urine for 2 days. He has had similar abdominal discomfort during the past 5 years, although he does not remember passing blood in the urine. He has had hypertension for the past 2 years, for which he has been prescribed medication. There is no history of weight loss, skin rashes, joint pain, vomiting, change in bowel habits, and smoking. On physical examination, there are ballotable flank masses bilaterally. The bowel sounds are normal. Renal function tests are as follows:
Urea 50 mg/dL
Creatinine 1.4 mg/dL
Protein Negative
RBC Numerous
The patient underwent ultrasonography of the abdomen, which revealed enlarged kidneys and multiple anechoic cysts with well-defined walls. What is the most likely diagnosis?

A CT scan confirmed the presence of multiple cysts in the kidneys.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient is a 34-year-old adult with bilateral flank masses, hypertension, hematuria, and multiple bilateral renal cysts on ultrasound, which is most consistent with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). ADPKD typically presents in adulthood with hypertension, hematuria, and progressively enlarging cystic kidneys. Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease usually presents in infancy or childhood, medullary cystic disease is associated with small kidneys and salt wasting, and acquired cystic kidney disease occurs in the setting of chronic kidney disease, especially in dialysis patients. The CT confirmation of multiple cysts further supports ADPKD.
Final answer: A

cue_condition.health.question: A 24-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal and lower back pain. She describes it as intense cramping and states that she experienced severe pain roughly 1 month ago that was similar. The patient's past medical history is non-contributory, and she states that her menses cause her to soak through 1 pad in a day. She is currently sexually active and does not use any contraception. Her vitals are within normal limits. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The patient's abdominal exam is non-focal, and her pelvic exam reveals no adnexal masses or tenderness and no cervical motion tenderness.

This presentation is most consistent with primary dysmenorrhea, which typically causes cyclic cramping pain without pelvic pathology. Appendicitis would usually cause focal right lower quadrant tenderness, ectopic pregnancy would typically show adnexal tenderness or mass and possible hemodynamic instability, and leiomyoma would often be associated with a palpable uterine mass or abnormal bleeding. The lack of pelvic findings and the cyclic nature of the pain support primary dysmenorrhea.

cue_condition.health.question: A 38-year-old man presents to the physician with fever and malaise for 4 days. He has headaches and joint pain. A pruritic rash appeared on the trunk yesterday. There is no history of serious illnesses or the use of medications. Ten days ago, he traveled to Brazil where he spent most of the time outdoors in the evenings. He did not use any control measures for mosquito bites. His temperature is 38.2℃ (100.8℉); the pulse is 88/min; the respiratory rate is 13/min, and the blood pressure is 125/60 mm Hg. Conjunctival suffusion is noted. A maculopapular rash is present over the trunk and proximal extremities without the involvement of the palms or soles. Several joints of the hands are tender to palpation. The abdomen is soft with no organomegaly. A peripheral blood smear shows no pathogenic organisms. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

He had blood in his ejaculate twice. His hearing has become partially impaired.

Blood in ejaculate (hematospermia) and hearing impairment are recognized but uncommon manifestations of Zika virus infection. Chagas disease typically presents with a chagoma or Romaña's sign and is transmitted by triatomine bugs, not mosquitoes. Malaria would show parasites on blood smear, and Rocky Mountain spotted fever typically involves the palms and soles.

cue_condition.health.question: A 70-year-old man is at his dermatologist’s office for the treatment of a severely pruritic erythroderma with scaling on his buttocks that has been slowly progressing over the past two weeks. The patient works as a truck driver and has a history of hypertension treated with enalapril. The patient reports having tried an over-the-counter cream on the rash without improvement. The vital signs are within normal range. On physical exam, he has multiple confluent and well-demarcated pink patches on his buttocks and legs with some scaling and enlarged inguinal lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?

The dermatologist orders a skin biopsy that reveals Pautrier microabscesses.

The patient's presentation of slowly progressive, pruritic erythroderma with scaling and enlarged inguinal lymph nodes is consistent with this diagnosis. Psoriasis, lichen planus, and atopic dermatitis do not typically show Pautrier microabscesses on biopsy.

cue_condition.health.question: A 28-year-old male presents to trauma surgery clinic after undergoing an exploratory laparotomy, femoral intramedullary nail, and femoral artery vascular repair 3 months ago. He suffered multiple gunshot wounds as a victim of a drive-by shooting. He is progressing well with well-healed surgical incisions on examination. He states that he has had difficulty sleeping and cannot concentrate when performing tasks. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

The patient experienced a traumatic event (multiple gunshot wounds) and now reports intrusive symptoms including nightmares and daytime flashbacks that relive the event, along with difficulty sleeping and concentrating. These symptoms have lasted 6 weeks, which is more than 1 month, meeting the duration criterion for PTSD. Schizophrenia and schizophreniform disorder are not supported because there are no psychotic symptoms such as delusions or hallucinations. A normal reaction to trauma would not include persistent re-experiencing symptoms lasting over a month.

cue_condition.health.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the physician by his parents because of a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight loss during the last 3 months. During this period, he has complained of abdominal pain and fullness, and his parents feel that he has been eating less. His parents also report that his urine has appeared pink for several weeks. He has been performing poorly in school lately, with reports from teachers that he has not been paying attention in class and has been distracting to other students. He was born at term and has been healthy except for a history of several infantile seizures. His vital signs are within normal limits. He is at the 60th percentile for height and 20th percentile for weight. Physical examination shows a palpable abdominal mass, abdominal tenderness in the left upper quadrant, and left costovertebral angle tenderness. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Consider this additional source evidence:
There are several ellipsoid, hypopigmented macules on the back and legs and a 4-cm raised plaque of rough, dimpled skin on the right lower back that is the same color as the surrounding skin.

reference_responses.intervention:
The boy has a palpable abdominal mass, pink urine (hematuria), and left upper quadrant/costovertebral angle tenderness, which suggests a renal angiomyolipoma or other renal lesion. The additional findings of hypopigmented macules (ash-leaf spots) and a shagreen patch are classic skin manifestations of tuberous sclerosis. Tuberous sclerosis is associated with renal angiomyolipomas, which can cause hematuria and abdominal pain. The history of infantile seizures and school difficulties also fits tuberous sclerosis, which commonly causes seizures and cognitive or behavioral issues.

cue_condition.health.question: A 64-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever presents to her primary care clinician complaining of excessive fatigue with walking and difficulty lying flat. She had no prior physical limitations, but recently has been unable to walk more than 3 blocks without needing to stop and rest. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Her cardiac exam is notable for a late diastolic murmur heard best at the apex in the left lateral decubitus position with no radiation.

reference_responses.intervention:
The late diastolic murmur at the apex with no radiation is characteristic of mitral stenosis, and the history of rheumatic fever is a common cause. Symptoms of exertional fatigue and difficulty lying flat are consistent with progressive mitral stenosis. Aortic stenosis typically produces a systolic ejection murmur, not a late diastolic murmur.
Final answer: B

cue_condition.health.question: A pregnant woman gives birth to her 1st child at the family farm. After delivery, the assisting midwife notices a triangular defect in the lower anterior abdominal wall of the baby. She clamps the umbilical cord with a cloth and urges the family to seek immediate medical care at the nearest hospital. No omphalocele is noted. The external genitalia is also affected. On physical exam, a shortened penis with a pronounced upward curvature and the urethral opening along the dorsal surface are also noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Consider this additional source evidence:
Upon admission, the attending pediatrician further notices an open bladder plate with an exposed urethra, a low set umbilicus, an anteriorly displaced anus, and an inguinal hernia.

reference_responses.intervention:
The baby has a lower anterior abdominal wall defect with an open bladder plate and exposed urethra, low-set umbilicus, and genital anomalies including a shortened penis with dorsal urethral opening and upward curvature. These findings are classic for bladder exstrophy, which involves the bladder and urethra opening onto the abdominal wall, often with epispadias and pubic diastasis. Cloacal exstrophy would also involve the hindgut and typically show omphalocele, which is absent here. Urachal cyst and posterior urethral valves do not present with an open bladder plate or abdominal wall defect.

cue_condition.health.question: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of an 8-month history of weakness and intermittent burning pain in her neck, shoulders, and arms. She was involved in a motor vehicle collision 1 year ago. Examination of the upper extremities shows absent reflexes, muscle weakness, and fasciculations bilaterally. The pupils are equal and reactive to light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

Consider this additional source evidence:
Sensation to temperature and pain is absent; vibration and proprioception are preserved.

reference_responses.intervention:
The patient has weakness, absent reflexes, muscle fasciculations, and dissociated sensory loss (absent pain and temperature with preserved vibration and proprioception) after trauma. This pattern is characteristic of syringomyelia, a fluid-filled cavity in the spinal cord that damages crossing spinothalamic fibers while sparing dorsal columns. Tabes dorsalis would cause sensory ataxia and loss of proprioception, ALS would show upper motor neuron signs, and cervical disk prolapse would not typically cause dissociated sensory loss.
Final answer: B

A 32-year-old Caucasian man presents to the physician because of the swelling and discomfort of the right testis for 3 weeks. There is no history of trauma, fever, or night sweats. He had surgery for an undescended right testis when he was 6 months old. There is no history of liver disease or hypogonadism. He has fathered 2 children. He takes no medications and denies any illicit drug use. The vital signs are within normal limits. Palpation of the scrotum reveals a firm nontender mass that cannot be separated from the right testis. Examination of the left testis shows no abnormalities. There is no supraclavicular or inguinal lymphadenopathy. Gynecomastia is present. The rest of the physical examination is unremarkable. Ultrasound shows an enlarged right testicle with a hypoechoic mass replacing a large portion of the normal architecture. The left testis is normal. The laboratory test results are as follows:

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

HCG Elevated
AFP Elevated
LDH Normal
